items.title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.original_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. Understanding its capabilities may help actuaries and risk professionals refine their approaches to strategy formulation.

items.rss_title: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating
items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Read the full interview > MORE ON PRICING & RATING Continuous Underwriting Wants to Scale by Riv Arthur Insurance premiums could fluctuate daily like stock prices, but regulation and reinsurance prevent the scaling of continuous underwriting. Read More Agentic AI Redefines Real-Time Underwriting by Rachita Nahata Real-time underwriting isn't about instant decisions but leveraging agentic AI and current data to help underwriters assess risk faster. Read More Breaking Down Silos in Insurance by Rory Meleniclis Insurers can dismantle organizational silos by shifting from project-based work to product teams built around shared capabilities like underwriting and claims. Read More How AI Can Transform Submissions for Underwriting by Prathap Gokul Commercial insurers face a strategic challenge: identifying which submissions merit scarce underwriting attention, not just processing more faster. Read More Making AI Work in Commercial Submission Intake by Vital Soupel Insurers need a practical blueprint for where to apply AI first, how to move beyond pilots, and how to scale the technology responsibly. Read More Turning Volatility Into Value by Inusrance Thought Leadership Amid today's heightened uncertainty, Dawn Miller, chief commercial officer at Lloyd's, explores how insurers can innovate their way to value both for themselves and for their clients. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

items.extracted_text: Cortina shows another avenue for third-party capital to enter the reinsurance market: Evercore ISI - Artemis.bm Cortina shows another avenue for third-party capital to enter the reinsurance market: Evercore ISI - Artemis.bm Cortina shows another avenue for third-party capital to enter the reinsurance market: Evercore ISI 11th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard A new report from Evercore ISI has outlined that the recently announced Aon and Blackstone reinsurance facility at Lloyd’s, Cortina, offers another alternative for third-party capital to be deployed into the reinsurance market without having to endure some of the exit risk mechanics. The much-discussed reinsurance Cortina syndicate 1956 was launched last week by broker Aon and funds associated with asset manager, Blackstone. At the same time, we also learned that the London Bridge 2 insurance-linked securities structure was also used towards funding the new syndicate. Cortina syndicate 1956 is expected to begin underwriting from January 1st, 2027, and is set to provide dedicated, multi-year reinsurance capacity to clients from institutional capital, adopting a conventional lead/follow approach. Global re/insurer QBE will also serve as managing agent of Cortina syndicate 1956, and be responsible for the syndicate’s underwriting and governance. Recall that we also reported last week that Cortina is set to bring $500 million of capital and write around $1.6 billion of premium . While this is small in comparison to the estimates $400 billion to $450 billion premium reinsurance marketplace, Evercore’s analysts explain in their report, that they expect it to scale in the future as other brokers launch similar vehicles that will serve to act as another softening force in the reinsurance pricing environment that already has excess capital. “However, we think Cortina and similar structures in the future could be a bit more disciplined than capital that entered in the past thru reinsurance start-ups that weren’t responsible underwriters,” Evercore ISI’s analysts explain. “Despite this, it is a negative for Reinsurers as it introduces more capacity to the finite risk pool and could open the way for more structures at other brokers with other asset managers,” analysts continued. While alternative capital, so that deployed through insurance-linked securities (ILS) and related collateralized structures, is small, estimated at around 3% of global premium, analysts emphasise that it holds potential for growth and for more pressure to be put on traditional reinsurers, although that market’s discipline has surprised Evercore ISI. For Aon, analysts stated that they expect Cortina to serve as a modest organic growth tailwind on volumes and market share, as it brings additional capacity at better pricing and on additional administration fees. As mentioned, analysts also suspect rival brokers to launch competing structures with other asset managers. “It will be interesting to see how much capital follows suit as we suspect other brokers launch similar structures. While third party capital has entered in the past via reinsurance startups, it appears like this is another avenue for that capital to enter without the exit risk,” analysts said. Large asset managers have increasingly shown that they prefer more flexible mechanisms to access reinsurance linked returns than standing up new equity backed companies, it’s expected this trend will continue developing often borrowing from ILS market infrastructure techniques. Concluding: “It is yet another sign of the softening market as more capacity enters which will weigh on pricing even if it is likely somewhat more responsible than start-up reinsurers in past cycles. items.extracted_text: Cat bond market primed for growth as perils, sponsors and capacity expands: Man Group - Artemis.bm Cat bond market primed for growth as perils, sponsors and capacity expands: Man Group - Artemis.bm Cat bond market primed for growth as perils, sponsors and capacity expands: Man Group 11th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard A new article from Man Group has highlighted how the catastrophe bond market continues to offer effective pricing competition, multi-year cover against a range of perils, and an additional source of capacity. All of which leads the firm to call out that it believes the market is well placed for further growth, provided pricing remains attractive to investors and sponsors. Authored by Andre Rzym, Partner and Portfolio Manager, Systematic, and Tarek Abou Zeid, Partner and Head of Client Portfolio Management, Systematic, the article explains that catastrophe bond returns have been positive every year since 2002, with double digit returns recorded in the last three years. The primary exception to this pattern occurred in 2022, when the Swiss Re Index declined by 2.15%. Major hurricane Ian was the main contributor towards that decline, with its impact amplified by the storm’s landfall in a densely populated area, while losses over the year were compounded by secondary perils, including floods and hailstorms. However, the authors importantly noted that this annual decline was an exception rather than the norm. Providing further context, the authors explain that a well-diversified cat bond portfolio may only hold one or two deals exposed to smaller perils. “In a portfolio of 100 equally weighted holdings, a triggering event may only result in a 1-2% loss. If the portfolio has a net expected annual return of 8%, such losses could be absorbed within a few months. Even for peak perils, to which more bonds are likely to be exposed, differences in geographical exposure, seniority, trigger type (such as an indemnity or industry index) and recovery basis (occurrence, aggregate) offer additional diversification,” the article reads. In addition, the authors underline that catastrophe bonds offer true diversification given that their low correlation with traditional assets is tied to natural disasters rather than financial market conditions. And as a result, unlike traditional assets that often fail to provide protection during severe market crashes, catastrophe bonds remain independent and hold their value when equities suffer major losses. Catastrophe bonds’ appeal to sponsors also goes beyond additional capacity. These financial instruments also support competitive pricing, limit counterparty exposure, and offer multi-year cover. “While traditional reinsurance usually has a one-year term, cat bonds commonly have terms of around three years. Sponsors can therefore secure multi-year cover, and some deals permit early termination,” the authors explain. Given the scale of benefits that the asset class provides for investors and sponsors, Man Group outlines that it believes the market appears well placed to grow without distorting the market price of risk. “Since 2002, the market’s capitalisation has grown from around USD0.5 billion to USD63 billion. Despite a four-year pause following the GFC, the market has grown steadily at about 23% per year. 2025 was a record year for issuance, and 2026 appears to be heading in the same direction,” Man Group said. “While growth has been impressive, cat bonds remain a much smaller market than many traditional financial assets, such as the US high-yield bond market which exceeds USD1 trillion. Provided cat bonds remain an attractive proposition, and as investor awareness and understanding develops, demand for these assets should continue to grow.” Further capacity into the market is likely to be drawn by several drivers. Man Group observes that climate change is likely to increase the scale of insured losses across the globe, noting that if insurer capital remains constant, more risk will then need to be ceded to reinsurers, and on to cat bonds. The firm also emphasised that the effects of inflation and urbanisation can increase insured losses, which will ultimately push up the amount of risk that needs to be ceded by insurers. With the frequency and severity of secondary perils constantly rising, more sponsors are turning to the cat bond market to secure protection. Therefore, this expanded capacity is, in turn, driving heightened investor interest towards the market too. Man Group also highlighted how the cat bond market has seen several transactions that cover cyber and terrorism risks. “The first terrorism-linked cat bond was launched in 2003. Golden Goal Finance provided cover in the event that the 2006 FIFA World Cup was cancelled, with terrorism among the risks contemplated. In 2019, Pool Re introduced pure UK terrorism cover to the market. GAREAT followed with French terrorism cover in 2024, and TRIP with US terrorism cover in 2026,” the authors said. “The first cyber cat bond deals, launched in 2023, were private, but these were closely followed by public deals later that year, and specialised cloud outage deals appeared in 2024.” Adding: “In our view, cyber could eventually become a third “peak peril”. Although we expect it to remain smaller than hurricanes and earthquakes, it could provide a valuable source of capacity (for sponsors) and diversification (for investors). We don’t expect terrorism cat bonds to reach the same scale but, given there are around 14 terrorism pools globally, we expect further growth.” The authors also observed that the cat bond space market constantly sees repeat sponsors, but underlined that new sponsors continue to enter the market, given their attraction to the competitive pricing and additional capacity that it offers. “The cat bond market has scope for further growth, and maintaining current premiums. Investors should be selective on deals and supportive of new perils as they arise,” Man Group said. Turning to the complexities of cat bond valuation and risk assessment, the authors state from time to time, certain perils or cat bonds that use parametric triggers are claimed to be underpriced, meaning that the spread offered is considered too low for the risk. “We are generally cautious about such claims. Cat bonds, by their nature, are designed to trigger infrequently, so a long and relevant history is needed to draw firm conclusions about event frequency. Moreover, an investor arguing that a new issue is underpriced must explain why its assessment of the risk differs from the price accepted in the market,” Man Group explained. Adding: “Investors who avoid risks they consider underpriced may benefit over the long term, but avoiding a single loss does not, by itself, demonstrate skill. Consider Hurricane Melissa in 2025, which triggered an International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) bond providing parametric cover to Jamaica. If an investor avoided that bond because they considered its spread too low, should avoiding the resulting loss count as alpha? At a higher spread, the same investor might have bought the bond and incurred the loss. The point is that the principal reduction on a single deal is independent of the spread that was paid. It is the expectation of the two that matters, and that requires much more data.” Another important feature that the author’s distinguish, is how the cat bond market is broadly ‘buy and hold’ in nature, with trading volumes typically higher in the primary market in comparison to the secondary market. As well as this, many catastrophe bond issuances are eligible for reporting and tracking through FINRA’s Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine (TRACE), making their transaction prices available for analysis. The author’s note that data shows that secondary-market volumes remain fairly steady throughout the year. By contrast, primary issuance, however, is seasonal and generally tends to slow down during the Atlantic hurricane season. For fund managers anticipating substantial inflows, this seasonal pattern may affect how quickly they can invest capital in new issuances. To conclude, the authors emphasise the dual value proposition driving the asset class forward. “For investors, the cat bond market has historically delivered equity-like returns with bond-like volatility over more than two decades. Because returns are primarily driven by physical events rather than market sentiment, and because premiums tend to harden after large losses, drawdowns have been both shallower and shorter than those of equities or bonds. items.extracted_text: Montauk Point hires Whiley to strengthen ILS Advisory & Special Situations - Artemis.bm Montauk Point hires Whiley to strengthen ILS Advisory & Special Situations - Artemis.bm Montauk Point hires Whiley to strengthen ILS Advisory & Special Situations 11th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Montauk Point Ltd., a Bermuda-based firm that provides independent advisory and strategic advice to third-party risk capital providers, has announced that senior ILS specialist John Whiley has joined the firm, where he will focus on strengthening its ILS Advisory and Special Situations capabilities. Recall that Montauk Point was launched in early 2025 by established reinsurance industry executive Adam Szakmary. Earlier this year, Montauk appointed 35-year insurance and reinsurance veteran Dr. Gero Michel to lead the company’s risk and analytics platform. The company continues to build-out its team, and has now announced the appointment of Bermuda ILS specialist John Whiley, who will primarily focus on ILS advisory, operational and governance support, and special situations involving portfolio transitions, restructurings, wind-downs and capital return strategies. Overall, Whiley brings over 25 years of extensive experience within investment management and administration, covering financial and regulatory reporting, governance, due diligence, and operational advisory. Most recently, Whiley held senior compliance roles at reinsurance linked asset manager Markel CATCo and Lodgepine Capital. He joined Markel CATCo in 2016 as Chief Compliance Officer, and stayed with the firm through the winding-down of the CATCo and Lodgepine funds. Prior to that, Whiley developed ILS administration solutions at Prime Management Limited, now part of SS&C Fund Services, which supported a significant proportion of Bermuda’s collateralized ILS fund market. Whiley’s appointment will help strengthen Montauk’s capabilities towards supporting insurance risk capital providers, investment managers and reinsurance entities. Adam Szakmary, President of Montauk, commented: “John brings extensive experience across Bermuda’s ILS market, particularly in fund operations, governance and complex wind-down situations. items.extracted_text: Our ability to invest consistently (in ILS) is a huge advantage: Quantedge CEO - Artemis.bm Our ability to invest consistently (in ILS) is a huge advantage: Quantedge CEO - Artemis.bm Our ability to invest consistently (in ILS) is a huge advantage: Quantedge CEO 10th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Quantedge Capital, the Singapore-based hedge fund asset manager, recognises that consistency in terms of its capital deployment to the insurance-linked securities asset class is key, as it enables the firm to be there when losses hit and it can benefit from hardening prices, CEO Suhaimi Zainul-Abidin explained in a recent podcast interview. Speaking with the Top Traders Unplugged podcast, Zainul-Abidin explained that how Quantedge Capital thinks about risk premia across all the asset classes it allocates to, which is helpful in understanding how the firm thinks about the ILS asset class and reinsurance. Quantedge manages approaching US $8 billion in its flagship systematic global hedge fund strategy, which has allocations across multiple asset classes such as equities, bonds, commodities, currencies and insurance-linked securities and had delivered a 20.9% net annualised return as of September 30th 2026. The hedge fund began allocating to ILS through catastrophe bonds in 2011, expanding its appetite out first to reinsurance sidecars and later to collateralized and fronted reinsurance or retrocession. ILS, as an asset class, exhibits all of the risk premia potential that Quantedge looks for and its CEO has even called ILS the purest form of risk premia in the past. He’s not a frequently heard from speaker though, particularly on this asset class, so we felt his comments during this podcast worth highlighting, to provide more of an insight into how the hedge fund manager feels about its ILS investments. During this podcast, Zainul-Abidin explained on risk premia, “A risk premia strategy is one which accepts risk essentially in exchange for an expected return. Right? So, we can think about it quite simply as what happens in an insurance contract. Every one of us, we buy insurance, you buy insurance, I do as well, to protect against risks that we don’t want to bear. And to hive off that risk, we’re willing to pay somebody to take it on. And typically, that would be the insurance company. “The insurance company, with all the knowledge and information and data that they have, know what is the fair price for that risk. But instead of charging you the fair price for it, they would charge you a premium. And that exists, obviously, in the insurance market. “But what we’ve noticed, based on our analysis and study of the markets, is actually that kind of risk transfer happens everywhere. In the equity markets, in the bond markets, commodity markets, there is always some kind of risk transfer. In fact, we think most markets exist for the purpose of risk transfer and that risk transfer could be just by virtue of being the capital provider taking on equity risk. But that kind of risk deserves a return, and the market adjusts itself to give participants the necessary return. So, we’re in all these markets trying to harvest this risk premia over time.” Quantedge Capital, typically known for being a systematic investor, still sees investing into the insurance-linked securities as having systematic qualities, even as most of the transactions entered into are privately negotiated. The CEO explained, “So, the systematic nature of the ILS investments that we do would be confined to the way that we analyse the deals. So, there’s a systematic way for us to decide how we want to allocate our risk budget to insurance linked securities and we want to achieve the same kind of diversification that we do in our general markets portfolio or general finance portfolio. “That means it’s hugely, hugely diversified across geographies, across perils. Meaning that we want to have exposure to hurricane risks, and earthquake risks, and wildfire risk, and cybersecurity risks, satellite risk, all sorts of things. We want to have great diversification. “In that respect, it’s systematic, but it is a market that is difficult to access. It is obviously not a public market. There are no exchanges to trade them on, which means there is an aspect of that business that is quite bespoke. We have to go to cedents and counterparties and negotiate deal by deal essentially.” Which of course also helps in starting to explain why the Quantedge CEO sees ILS as an asset class to be consistent in. Zainul-Abidin explained the return potential of the ILS and reinsurance asset class, “It varies from year to year, like any market and we’d analyse the expected returns from ILS on a year-to-year basis. It really depends on the amount of capital that’s going to the markets, the risk aversion, whether or not there’s been a catastrophe event that has maybe sometimes sucked money out of the markets the previous year. So, a lot of factors go into it but we would expect, in some years, and in fact over the long term, that you could get potentially 20% returns on cash, which is pretty healthy, pretty juicy.” Quantedge Capital recognises that its investments into ILS and reinsurance will take losses over-time and having been in the asset class since 2011 the hedge fund will have taken its share, but being there to provide capital to the industry following loss activity is one of the benefits of a consistent approach. Zainul-Abidin acknowledged that losses will happen, “Of course, absolutely and it doesn’t look pretty when it happens. But that’s the nature of risk premia. Right? Over time you get paid out, but you get paid out exactly because you’re willing to bear that risk and from time to time take the hit. So, a lot of the strategies within our portfolio have those kinds of characteristics. “It’s like investing in the equity markets. From time to time there is going to be a big correction, and the markets are paying you to take that risk. That is the nature of risk premia. “But we want to be in that space. In fact, I think our ability to invest consistently through those kinds of ups and downs gives us a huge advantage. Because if you notice, particularly in the ILS space, whenever something bad materialises and all the risk takers take a hit because there’s a sizable loss, you will see that capital drains out of the market the following year. But as a result of that, the premiums go up a lot. So, we want to be there for when that happens.” You can find the full Top Traders Unplugged podcast episode here . items.extracted_text: California Earthquake Authority lifts Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond to target $900m of reinsurance - Artemis.bm California Earthquake Authority lifts Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond to target $900m of reinsurance - Artemis.bm California Earthquake Authority lifts Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond to target $900m of reinsurance 11th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans The California Earthquake Authority (CEA) is aiming to meaningfully upsize its latest catastrophe bond sponsorship, with the target for the issuance raised 50% to now $900 million of fully-collateralized earthquake reinsurance limit from the new Ursa Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) transaction, Artemis understands. The California Earthquake Authority (CEA) returned to the catastrophe bond market in late October, with an initial target to secure $600 million of reinsurance protection from its latest cat bond sponsorship. Given market conditions and how conducive the pricing environment is for sponsors of cat bonds at this time, it’s no surprise to learn the CEA is looking to increase the amount of reinsurance limit from its latest deal, while we’re told it is also targeting lower pricing for the protection as well. The CEA has $2.875 billion of outstanding catastrophe bond coverage still in-force at this time and currently sits in 4th place in our cat bond sponsors leaderboard . When we last reported on the CEA’s reinsurance risk transfer tower, the earthquake insurer had limit of just over $8.2 billion in-force at the end of April 2026 , with the catastrophe bond market providing around 35% of that total. This new Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond will become the 25th visit to the market by the California Earthquake Authority (CEA) we have tracked. View details of every catastrophe bond sponsored by the CEA in the Artemis Deal Directory . With the latest update to this deal, Ursa Re Ltd. is now offering $900 million of notes across the two tranches of this Series 2026-1 cat bond issuance, up from the initial $600 million target. The goal is to secure the CEA a now larger, roughly four year source of fully-collateralized California earthquake reinsurance protection on an indemnity trigger and annual aggregate basis. What was initially a $350 million Series 2026-1 Class D tranche of notes are now offered at $500 million in size, we are told. The Class D notes have an initial expected loss of 2.68% and they were first offered to investors with price guidance in a range from 4% to 4.5%. That price guidance has now fallen to a revised range of 3.75% to 4%, we understand. The initially $250 million Series 2026-1 Class H tranche of notes are now offered at $400 million in size. The Class H notes come with an initial expected loss of 6.35% and were first offered to investors with price guidance in a range from 8.5% to 9.5%. That price guidance has also been revised lower, at 8.25% to 8.5%, sources explained. As we said in our first article on this new Ursa Re 2026-1 catastrophe bond, we believe the Class H notes have the highest expected loss for any tranche of catastrophe bonds that we have seen sponsored by the CEA. At a $900 million issuance size, according to Artemis’ data this new cat bond for the CEA is now targeted to be its largest since 2017 and the earthquake insurers second largest cat bond sponsorship ever. You can read all about this new Ursa Re Ltd. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.extracted_text: People Moves: Island Insurance Names Cheung VP Alliant Names Shenouda AI Transformation Officer Daley Becomes EverPeak CUO Article 0 Comments Cheung Joins Island Insurance as VP of Operations, Data and Product Management Michelle Cheung Island Insurance named Michelle Cheung to its executive team as vice president overseeing the organization’s operations and data products management. Most recently, Cheung was the IT development manager at American Savings Bank. Other previous positions include founder and executive director at the nonprofit TRUE Initiative senior vice president of marketing, research & technology at Locations LLC and vice president at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi UFJ and Citigroup. Island Insurance is headquartered in Honolulu, Hawaii. Alliant Names Shenouda as Divisional COO and AI Transformation Officer Alliant Underwriting Solutions , the program administrator division of Alliant Insurance Services, named Shaun Shenouda divisional chief operating officer and AI transformation officer. Shenouda will lead AUS’ efforts in artificial intelligence and automation, including prioritizing initiatives, committing resources and driving innovation. Shenouda will continue his role as president of AUS company SES Risk Solutions, a property/casualty insurance provider serving portfolios of single-family residential rental properties and properties held in trust by financial institutions. Alliant is headquartered in Irvine, California. EverPeak Names Daley CUO EverPeak named Patrick K. Daley chief underwriting officer. Daley will lead underwriting strategy and quality standards across EverPeak’s lines of business. Daley has more than three decades of experience underwriting large, complex, and hard-to-place risks at carriers including Zurich Insurance, The Hartford, and GuideOne Insurance. Most recently, Daley was head of underwriting services at Glatfelter Insurance Group. Before that, as CUO of GuideOne Insurance. Early in his career, he held underwriting roles at Swiss Re, CNA Re, GE Insurance, and Chubb. EverPeak is headquartered in Denver, Colorado. items.title: Same Goal, Different Pressures: Building Managed Repair Partnerships on Mutual Understanding
items.original_title: Same Goal, Different Pressures: Building Managed Repair Partnerships on Mutual Understanding
items.rss_title: Same Goal, Different Pressures: Building Managed Repair Partnerships on Mutual Understanding
items.rss_description: The premise of managed repair is straightforward: rather than insurance carriers reimbursing policyholders directly for property damage, carriers refer claims to a managed repair program. The MRP coordinates documentation of the repairs necessary to return the structure to its preloss …
items.extracted_text: Same Goal, Different Pressures: Building Managed Repair Partnerships on Mutual Understanding Article 0 Comments The premise of managed repair is straightforward: rather than insurance carriers reimbursing policyholders directly for property damage, carriers refer claims to a managed repair program. The MRP coordinates documentation of the repairs necessary to return the structure to its preloss condition and, where selected by the property owner to effect those repairs, oversees repairs through a network of preapproved, vetted contractors. But as much as all stakeholders in the managed repair ecosystem share a common desire to restore policyholders’ homes, lives and businesses, the underlying concerns and priorities that each is grappling with can be worlds apart. As a third-party administrator, we have a vantage point on this disconnect — and on the importance of mitigating it. We know that the pressures contractors absorb today could show up tomorrow in cycle times, estimate accuracy and the policyholder experience. So, in the interest of increased understanding, we recently asked our network of insurance restoration professionals to share what’s really happening inside their businesses. The takeaway for property claims leaders is not just in what contractors told us, but in what their feedback may indicate about the challenges and opportunities ahead. Lance Malcolm Cost of Doing Business: The Defining Concern for Restoration Businesses Today Operating pressures, including project delays, cancellations, safety concerns and escalating insurance-related costs, were recurring themes throughout contractor feedback, with rising material costs, economic uncertainty and labor shortages topping contractors’ list of worries. Material costs especially stood out because concern about them was nearly identical in every U.S. region, emphasizing that this is an industrywide structural pressure rather than a short-term, geography-specific issue. None of these trends were particularly surprising given current headlines, but what’s interesting is how contractors are handling them. When asked how the labor market is affecting their pricing, 58% said they have absorbed higher labor costs to keep their prices steady, yet only about a third have raised prices on their jobs. That pattern holds in every region and at every firm size, from two-person outfits to shops with more than 100 employees. Although steady job pricing may sound like good news for carriers, the rising underlying costs contractors are facing create an increasingly unsustainable model for the managed repair ecosystem. If contractors continue to absorb higher operational expenses without corresponding pricing adjustments, the industry could see mounting labor challenges, longer project timelines, greater strain on the customer experience and increased pressure on contractor profitability. Over time, these dynamics may contribute to network contraction as some firms scale back operations or exit the market altogether. Impact of The Labor Market Can Be Felt Well Beyond Pricing Nearly nine in 10 (86%) insurance restoration contractors said the labor market is affecting their business. More than half find it harder to hire qualified workers, and a similar percentage report rising wage expectations. The effects extend well into contractors’ day-to-day operations. The most common result is longer job cycle times, followed by effects on pricing and their ability to scale projects. For claims leaders, the real concern here is cycle time, as faster repairs ultimately drive policyholder satisfaction. It’s worth noting that the labor market impacts felt by contractors vary by geography. Labor shortages are the top concern in the Northeast and Midwest but barely register in the Southwest and West, where economic uncertainty leads instead. The size of the firm matters too, as midsized firms with 26 to 75 employees are more than twice as likely as smaller firms to name safety and insurance pressures as their biggest concern. The question for the industry is how to create the flexibility needed to sustain a healthy managed repair ecosystem while continuing to drive consistency, estimate accuracy and customer outcomes. Managed repair stakeholders, including carriers, networks and contractors, each play an important role in controlling loss adjustment expense through disciplined documentation, transparent estimating practices and effective repair oversight. Absent that flexibility, contractors may increasingly pursue alternative business opportunities, reducing available network capacity and making it more difficult to deliver the estimating expertise, repair quality and policyholder experience carriers have come to expect. Increased Industry Collaboration Unsurprisingly, nearly every contractor we surveyed uses technology only eight of 473 said they don’t. The most common uses are cost estimation and scoping, communications and documentation, and project management. Contractors are also adopting tools in the field for drying and remediation, moisture detection, and damage assessment. This is encouraging. Estimation and documentation have historically been the points where carriers and contractors get stuck in back-and-forth. Shared digital workflows such as real-time photo documentation, live video and consistent estimating platforms can shorten review cycles, improve indemnity accuracy and cut the friction that frustrates adjusters and contractors alike. The industry is also seeing how technology can help bridge this gap. Solutions that improve estimate quality, accelerate review workflows, increase project visibility and leverage AI-assisted decision support are reducing friction across the claims and restoration process. Understanding Must be Followed by Action To strengthen the managed repair process, carriers must not only understand the burdens their restoration partners face but also collaborate on solutions that benefit the industry as a whole. We’ve taken the first step with the 2026 Managed Repair Market Report , but acknowledging the state of the industry can’t be the end of the story. Carriers and program partners must now use these insights to make smarter decisions for the future. Managed repair depends on effective coordination among carriers, contractors and policyholders. As carriers shape their future claims and vendor strategies, these market dynamics should be an important consideration in strategic planning to help preserve network capacity, sustain performance and continue delivering the customer experience policyholders expect. items.rss_title: Terror Suit Against Drugmakers Draws US Supreme Court Inquiry
items.rss_description: The U.S. Supreme Court asked the Trump administration for input on an appeal from pharmaceutical and medical-device companies that are trying to stop a lawsuit accusing them of helping to finance terrorist attacks in Iraq. The companies are seeking review …
items.extracted_text: Terror Suit Against Drugmakers Draws US Supreme Court Inquiry Article 0 Comments The U.S. Supreme Court asked the Trump administration for input on an appeal from pharmaceutical and medical-device companies that are trying to stop a lawsuit accusing them of helping to finance terrorist attacks in Iraq. The companies are seeking review of a ruling that let American terrorism victims sue the companies for allegedly paying millions of dollars in bribes to secure medical-supply contracts with the Iraqi Ministry of Health from 2004 to 2013. The victims say the money went to Jaysh al-Mahdi, a militant group that controlled the ministry. The lawsuit names units of AstraZeneca Plc, Roche Holding Ltd., GE HealthCare Technologies Inc., Johnson & Johnson, Pfizer Inc. and Viatris Inc. as defendants. The companies were sued by servicemembers and civilians who served in Iraq, as well as their families. The justices directed their request Monday to U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top Supreme Court lawyer. The companies say they contracted with the ministry at the encouragement of the U.S. government. They told the Supreme Court that, even if true, the allegations against them weren’t sufficient to let a lawsuit go forward under the U.S. Anti-Terrorism Act. The drugmakers said the suit didn’t allege a sufficiently close connection between their transactions with the ministry and specific acts of terrorism. The companies also contended the law requires a showing that a defendant intended to help a terror attack succeed. In urging the Supreme Court to reject the appeal, the victims said the companies knew their bribes financed attacks and yet continued paying for years. A federal appeals court in Washington ruled the suit could go forward, saying the complaint adequately alleged that the companies repeatedly structured their transactions in an unusual and illegal manner that facilitated Jaysh al-Mahdi’s activities. The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in 2023 that the Anti-Terrorism Act couldn’t be used to hold social media companies responsible for a 2017 shooting in an Istanbul nightclub. Both sides in the Iraq case contended the court’s reasoning in the 2023 case supported their arguments. The case is AstraZeneca U.K. v. Atchley , 26-245. items.extracted_text: AM Best Revises Outlook to Stable for Members of Texas Farm Bureau Insurance Group Article 0 Comments AM Best has revised the outlook to stable from negative for the Long-Term Issuer Credit Ratings (Long-Term ICRs) and affirmed the Financial Strength Rating (FSR) of B++ (Good) and the Long-Term ICRs of “bbb+” (Good) for the members of Texas Farm Bureau Insurance Group. The outlook of the FSR is stable. All companies are domiciled in Waco, Texas. The ratings reflect Texas Farm Bureau Insurance Group’s balance sheet strength, which AM Best assesses as strong, as well as its marginal operating performance, neutral business profile and appropriate enterprise risk management (ERM). The revision of the outlook to stable from negative for the Long-Term ICRs reflects improvement in the group’s recent operating performance metrics driven by management’s various initiatives including rate increases and underwriting refinement, as well as more benign weather. The stable outlooks reflect AM Best’s expectation that volatility will remain within manageable levels in the intermediate term, despite the group’s inherent weather-related exposure. items.extracted_text: Liberty Mutual Investments Backs Pet and Vet Services Firm Synergy Pet Group Article 0 Comments Liberty Mutual Investments, the investment firm for Liberty Mutual Group, said it has provided debt financing to Synergy Pet Group to support the company’s continued pet services and technology expansion. Synergy Pet Group, based in Lakewood, New Jersey, is backed by LoneTree Capital, which made a growth investment in the company in 2023. LMI also invested in Synergy in 2023 alongside LoneTree. Synergy Pet Group offers a range of pet services and technology for pet owners, employers, brokers, and veterinary practices. Through its Wishbone family of brands, (Total Pet, Insurance and Wellness), the company provides pet-related employee benefits, pet insurance programs, and other services designed to make pet care more accessible and affordable. Synergy has expanded into veterinary technology through Shepherd Veterinary Solutions, a veterinary practice management system. “This financing gives us the flexibility to invest in our businesses while staying focused on execution,” said Charles Nebenzahl, CEO of Synergy Pet Group. “Synergy Pet Group has built an exceptional platform at the center of the growing pet care economy, combining its market-leading pet benefits business with an innovative veterinary technology offering in Shepherd,” said Alex Kayvanfar, head of Capital Solutions at LMI. items.rss_title: Indiana AG: Rental Home Operator to Pay $48M Settlement
items.rss_description: Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita on Tuesday announced a settlement with Progress Residential, LLC and Pretium Partners, LLC, one of the nation’s largest owners and operators of single-family rental homes, resolving allegations that the companies engaged in deceptive and unfair …
items.extracted_text: Indiana AG: Rental Home Operator to Pay $48M Settlement Article 0 Comments Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita on Tuesday announced a settlement with Progress Residential, LLC and Pretium Partners, LLC, one of the nation’s largest owners and operators of single-family rental homes, resolving allegations that the companies engaged in deceptive and unfair practices affecting renters, including Indiana residents. The settlement provides $48.5 million in monetary relief for consumers nationwide and requires sweeping reforms to the companies’ business practices. According to Attorney General Rokita, his office joined the bipartisan enforcement action alongside the Federal Trade Commission, the Arizona Attorney General, the Colorado Attorney General, and the Utah Division of Consumer Protection. The complaint, filed in the United States District Court in the Northern District of Georgia, alleged that the defendants advertised rental prices that did not reflect the actual cost tenants were required to pay, imposed hidden and improperly disclosed fees, mishandled security deposits, misrepresented the condition of rental properties, restricted consumer reviews, and failed to adequately address tenant complaints and maintenance issues. The agreement contains no admission of wrongdoing by Progress. “Although we disagree with the FTC’s claims, this resolution allows us to move forward with our mission of expanding access to quality, affordable rental housing in neighborhoods of opportunity,” Progress said in a statement. Under the settlement, the companies must make significant changes to their business practices that will benefit tenants in Indiana and across the country. items.extracted_text: Nvidia-Backed Fireworks AI Notifies Customers of Its Second Hack in Weeks Article 0 Comments Fireworks AI, a popular startup that helps companies run artificial intelligence models, notified customers on Monday of a security breach in which their data was accessed, its second known hack in a matter of weeks. A Fireworks spokesperson said the company is “actively working with our customers to manage the incident, including Notion, Cursor and others.” Fireworks has over 10,000 customers, including the legal tech firm Harvey, productivity software startup Notion and coding company Cursor, according to its website. Fireworks said in a blog post that an unauthorized third-party breached an external cloud provider that hosts the company’s machines. The breach included tens of thousands of files that contained customer data in some cases, according to a person familiar with the matter. This incident happened on Oct. 24, Fireworks said. In early October, Fireworks AI disclosed a different security incident that involved unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials to get access to a number of customer accounts. At the time, the startup said it was investigating the matter and working with a cybersecurity firm “to assist with the incident.” On Monday, Fireworks AI confirmed in the post that its investigation of the early October breach uncovered impacts to customers’ account and billing information. In addition, the inquiry found that for a limited set of accounts, the breach impacted “secrets, datasets and incomplete models.” The startup said evidence links a cybercriminal threat actor group to the early October incident. After identifying security issues involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, Fireworks launched an investigation with support from the cybersecurity firm Palo Alto Networks Inc. and notified law enforcement, the startup said in a statement. “We take this matter very seriously and are connecting directly with customers to provide appropriate support,” the company added. Fireworks didn’t provide information about who was responsible for the latest incident. Fireworks’ backers include Nvidia Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. The startup was last valued at $17.5 billion in July and is in discussions for a new round of funding at between a $30 billion and $40 billion valuation, people familiar with the matter said. items.title: Maryland High Court Weighs Sovereign Immunity Claim for Some Sex Abuse Lawsuits
items.original_title: Maryland High Court Weighs Sovereign Immunity Claim for Some Sex Abuse Lawsuits
items.rss_title: Maryland High Court Weighs Sovereign Immunity Claim for Some Sex Abuse Lawsuits
items.rss_description: Maryland’s highest court heard arguments on an appeal Monday that will affect 1,300 lawsuits filed under the Child Victims Act. The 2023 law effectively eliminated time barriers for someone to file a court claim of institutional sex abuse. At issue …
items.extracted_text: Maryland High Court Weighs Sovereign Immunity Claim for Some Sex Abuse Lawsuits Article 0 Comments Maryland’s highest court heard arguments on an appeal Monday that will affect 1,300 lawsuits filed under the Child Victims Act. The 2023 law effectively eliminated time barriers for someone to file a court claim of institutional sex abuse. At issue are the roughly 1,300 cases in which the alleged sexual assaults took place before 1982, a time when the state had absolute immunity from lawsuits. The Supreme Court of Maryland is being asked to decide if the General Assembly, when it passed the landmark 2023 law, clearly and knowingly waived that immunity. The article is republished from Maryland Matters . Jonathan Massey, attorney for a plaintiff known only as J.C., said the waiver of damage caps in the 2023 law are proof of the legislature’s intent. The change “is the waiver of state sovereign immunity, and make changes that assume there will be a damages cap, assuming there will be liability to the state, right? That’s why you need a damages cap because there’s going to be liability to the state. I don’t think the legislature was silent in 2023 on the issue of sovereign immunity,” Massey said during oral arguments. Monday’s appeal involves a claim of sexual abuse from 1977, when J.C. was a patient at the old Prince George’s Hospital Center, where she claimed a doctor molested her during a stay there. Lawyers for the state argued that the state at the time was protected by sovereign immunity. Prior to 1982, the state could not face civil lawsuits, and the state’s lawyers asked a Prince George’s County judge to dismiss the case on those grounds. Attorneys representing the state filed roughly 200 motions to dismiss cases involving claims before July 1, 1982. The state has argued that the legislature must expressly waive the 40-year old immunity provision, something they said the 2023 law did not do. Judges at the Circuit Court level granted four motions at the time the appeal was filed with the state’s highest court. The Prince George’s County court denied the state’s motion without a hearing or explanation. But judges in Frederick County and Baltimore City have agreed with the state. Each dismissed cases under the sovereign immunity argument. The Supreme Court’s ruling on the issue comes with a dollar sign attached. Cases involving allegations occurring before 1982 comprise about 11% of the 12,000 cases that have been filed under the Child Victims Act. The 2023 law capped damages against the state at $890,000 per occurrence, but the definition of an “occurrence” is still being debated. The full extent of the state’s potential liability has never been publicly stated. A rough estimate shows potentially budget-busting consequences. If each plaintiff alleged just one occurrence and received the maximum award, the potential liability to the state could be about $11 billion. That estimate is nearly four times the structural budget gap projected for the fiscal 2028 budget to be introduced in January. The potential payout could go up if a court or jury defines “occurrence” as each instance of abuse, rather than bundling instances based on any number of related circumstances. Settlements could reduce the potential liability. If lawyers for the state are successful in getting the pre-1982 cases blocked, it would reduce the state’s potential liability by “more than a billion dollars,” the Office of the Attorney General argued in a filing earlier this year. During the nearly hour-long oral arguments Monday, justices seemed focused on whether the Child Victims Act waived sovereign immunity in an “unambiguous manner.” And if that was not the case, could legislative intent be used to rule that the General Assembly had in fact waived the immunity. “If their intent was to undo sovereign immunity, isn’t it a little odd that they didn’t mention it?” Chief Justice Matthew Fader asked Massey during the hearing. Massey argued that the General Assembly made it clear through setting caps and through its debates that it understood what it was doing and the potential costs. But Fader wondered aloud if anyone in the legislature was aware of the immunity which ended in the 1980s and the passage of the Maryland Tort Claims Act. “What it doesn’t necessarily indicate to me is an intent to undo a sovereign immunity protection that they seemingly were just unaware of,” Fader said. “And if that’s the case, if they thought that liability would go back before 1982 because they just weren’t aware that there was a sovereign immunity protection in place, that doesn’t seem to me to be an an intent to undo that sovereign immunity protection. It’s just an unawareness of it.” Ryan Dietrich, an assistant attorney general, told the justices that nothing in the law could be interpreted as a waiver. Legislative intent would not be enough. “I think what we heard from a friend on the other side about the legislative history is they say we think, we assume, and when we think and when we assume, that’s hallmarks of ambiguity,” Dietrich said. “To the extent that the legislature did not speak clearly, unambiguously, and expressly, this court must err on the side of saying that sovereign immunity has not been waived, and send it back to the legislature to say, ‘What did you really mean?'” he said.
